blocks.content: Shortest Job First is not just another scheduling policy chosen by convention. It is the algorithm that provably minimizes the average waiting time of every process in the ready queue, a mathematical guarantee that very few scheduling algorithms can claim. This chapter explores both its non-preemptive form, called SJF, and its preemptive cousin, Shortest Remaining Time First, called SRTF, along with the very practical problem that keeps this theoretically optimal algorithm from being used exactly as described in most real systems.

We will work through a fully numeric example of SJF and place it side by side with FCFS on the exact same processes, watch SRTF preempt a running process the moment a shorter one arrives, look honestly at why both algorithms need information that is impossible to know for certain in advance, and see how starvation quietly becomes their price for being so efficient.
1. The Problem SJF Is Trying to Solve
blocks.text: 1. The Problem SJF Is Trying to Solve

blocks.content: First Come First Served runs processes strictly in the order they arrive, with no regard for how long each one will take. That simplicity has a cost, widely known as the convoy effect, where a single long process at the front of the queue forces every short process behind it to sit and wait, dragging down the average waiting time for everyone. Shortest Job First takes the opposite approach. Instead of asking who arrived first, it asks a more useful question: who will finish fastest, and lets that process go first.

blocks.title: Recap: the convoy effect
blocks.content: FCFS lets order of arrival decide everything, so one long process ahead of several short ones can hold up the entire queue behind it, much like a slow truck holding up traffic on a single lane road. SJF is designed specifically to avoid this.
2. Shortest Job First, SJF, Explained

SJF is a non-preemptive algorithm. Among all the processes currently sitting in the ready queue, the scheduler always picks the one with the shortest burst time to run next. Once that process is chosen and starts running, it runs to completion without interruption, even if a process with an even shorter burst time arrives while it is still executing. The scheduler only makes a new choice once the current process finishes and the processor becomes free again.
How the scheduler chooses

["Look at every process currently waiting in the ready queue.","Compare their burst times, the amount of CPU time each one needs to finish.","Pick the process with the smallest burst time and run it to completion.","Once it finishes, repeat the comparison among whatever is left in the queue."]
items: Look at every process currently waiting in the ready queue.
Compare their burst times, the amount of CPU time each one needs to finish.
Pick the process with the smallest burst time and run it to completion.
Once it finishes, repeat the comparison among whatever is left in the queue.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: SJF always runs the shortest available job next, and never interrupts a job once it has started.
3. A Fully Worked Example: SJF Against FCFS
blocks.text: 3. A Fully Worked Example: SJF Against FCFS

blocks.content: Consider four processes that all arrive at the same moment, time zero, with the following burst times.
Running them with SJF
Since every process arrives at the same instant, SJF simply sorts them by burst time and runs the shortest first: P4, then P1, then P3, then P2.
Average waiting time under SJF equals the sum of the waiting times divided by the number of processes: zero plus three plus nine plus sixteen, divided by four, which comes to seven time units.
The same four processes under FCFS
blocks.text: The same four processes under FCFS

blocks.content: Now run the identical four processes under FCFS, in their arrival order P1, P2, P3, P4.
Average waiting time under FCFS is zero plus six plus fourteen plus twenty one, divided by four, which comes to ten point two five time units.

Same four processes, same total work, yet SJF brings the average waiting time down from ten point two five time units to seven time units, an improvement of more than thirty percent, purely by changing the order in which they run.
4. Shortest Remaining Time First, SRTF, Explained
blocks.text: 4. Shortest Remaining Time First, SRTF, Explained

blocks.content: SRTF is the preemptive version of SJF. The rule sounds almost identical, but one word changes everything: whenever a new process arrives in the ready queue, the scheduler compares that new arrival's burst time against the remaining time of the process currently running on the processor. If the new arrival needs less time than what is left of the current process, the scheduler preempts the running process immediately, pauses it, and switches the processor to the new arrival. The paused process goes back into the ready queue and will be picked up again later based on its remaining time, not its original burst time.

["A running process keeps the processor only as long as no shorter job is waiting.","Every new arrival triggers a fresh comparison, not just processes that arrive at time zero.","A preempted process does not lose its progress, only its turn. It resumes later exactly where it left off.","Because comparisons happen continuously, SRTF reacts faster to short jobs than non-preemptive SJF, at the cost of extra context switches."]
items: A running process keeps the processor only as long as no shorter job is waiting.
Every new arrival triggers a fresh comparison, not just processes that arrive at time zero.
A preempted process does not lose its progress, only its turn. It resumes later exactly where it left off.
Because comparisons happen continuously, SRTF reacts faster to short jobs than non-preemptive SJF, at the cost of extra context switches.

blocks.title: SJF versus SRTF in one line
blocks.content: SJF decides once, when a process is chosen, and never looks back. SRTF keeps checking after every arrival and is willing to change its mind.
5. A Worked Example: Watching SRTF Preempt Mid-Execution
blocks.text: 5. A Worked Example: Watching SRTF Preempt Mid-Execution

blocks.content: Consider four processes that this time arrive at different moments.
Tracing the execution second by second
blocks.text: Tracing the execution second by second

blocks.content: P1 is the only process in the system at time zero, so it starts running. At time one, P2 arrives with a burst time of four. P1 has already run for one time unit out of its eight, so it has seven time units remaining. The scheduler compares P2's burst time of four against P1's remaining time of seven, and since four is smaller, P1 is preempted immediately and P2 takes over the processor. This is the interruption to watch closely: P1 is paused after just one time unit of work, with seven time units still left to run later.

At time two, P3 arrives with a burst time of nine. P2 has been running for one time unit and has three time units remaining. Nine is larger than three, so no preemption happens and P2 keeps running. At time three, P4 arrives with a burst time of five. P2 now has two time units remaining, and five is larger than two, so P2 again keeps running. P2 finishes at time five, having run for its full four time units without any further interruption after it took over from P1.

With P2 finished, the scheduler looks at everyone left in the ready queue: P1 with seven time units remaining, P3 with nine time units remaining, and P4 with five time units remaining, its full burst time since it has not run yet. P4 is shortest, so it runs to completion from time five to time ten. Only P1 and P3 remain, and P1's seven time units are shorter than P3's nine, so P1 resumes from time ten and runs to completion at time seventeen. Finally P3 runs alone from time seventeen to time twenty six.

blocks.content: Average waiting time under SRTF is nine plus zero plus fifteen plus two, divided by four, which comes to six point five time units. SRTF's average waiting time is always less than or equal to what non-preemptive SJF would produce on the same set of processes, because SRTF can react the instant a shorter process shows up instead of waiting for the processor to become free.
6. The Practical Limitation: You Have To Know The Future
blocks.text: 6. The Practical Limitation: You Have To Know The Future

blocks.content: Both SJF and SRTF share one serious, unavoidable problem: to pick the shortest job, the scheduler must already know each process's burst time before that process even starts running. In a real operating system this is genuinely impossible to know for certain. A process might read a small file and finish in milliseconds, or it might loop for hours depending on input the scheduler cannot see in advance. Burst time is not printed anywhere on the process; it only becomes known after the fact, once the process has already finished.
Estimating the future from the past
blocks.text: Estimating the future from the past

blocks.content: Since the true burst time cannot be known in advance, real implementations settle for a prediction instead. The most common technique is exponential averaging, which estimates a process's next burst time as a weighted blend of its previous estimate and how long its most recent burst actually took. Recent history counts more than distant history, so the estimate adapts as a process's behavior changes, while a single unusual burst does not throw the prediction off completely. Processes that have consistently run for a short time in the past are predicted to be short again, and the scheduler treats that prediction as if it were the real burst time.

blocks.title: The idea without the formula
blocks.content: Think of it as a running average that leans more heavily on the most recent measurement. If a process has always finished quickly before, the scheduler bets it will finish quickly again, and updates that bet slightly after every burst.
7. Starvation: The Other Serious Flaw

SJF and SRTF fix the convoy effect, but they introduce a problem of their own. A process with a genuinely long burst time can be skipped over again and again by a steady stream of shorter processes arriving after it. Every time the scheduler looks at the ready queue, some newer, shorter job looks more attractive, so the long process keeps getting pushed back and may wait an extremely long time before it ever gets to run. This is effectively the mirror image of the convoy effect: FCFS punishes short jobs by making them wait behind one long one, while SJF and SRTF can punish a long job by making it wait behind an endless supply of short ones.

blocks.title: Forward pointer
blocks.content: The common fix for starvation is called aging, where a process's priority quietly increases the longer it waits, eventually guaranteeing it a turn. Aging is covered in full in the Priority Scheduling chapter, since starvation is really a general problem with any scheduler that always prefers one kind of process over another.

9. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 9. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: Common mistakes

["Confusing burst time with arrival time. SJF and SRTF pick the next process by comparing burst time or remaining time, never by who arrived earliest, that is what FCFS does.","Checking for preemption only when a process starts running. SRTF must compare the remaining time of the running process against every single new arrival, not just the very first process in the queue, otherwise a legitimate preemption gets missed."]
items: Confusing burst time with arrival time. SJF and SRTF pick the next process by comparing burst time or remaining time, never by who arrived earliest, that is what FCFS does.

Checking for preemption only when a process starts running. SRTF must compare the remaining time of the running process against every single new arrival, not just the very first process in the queue, otherwise a legitimate preemption gets missed.

blocks.content: The interview angle

Interviewers like SJF and SRTF because the questions write themselves: prove that SJF minimizes average waiting time, trace through a Gantt chart by hand, or explain why an operating system cannot actually run SJF exactly as textbooks describe it. The strongest answers do three things: state the optimality result confidently, work through a concrete numeric trace without mixing up burst time and remaining time, and immediately raise the burst time prediction problem and starvation as the reasons real schedulers only approximate SJF rather than use it outright. Showing that you understand both why SJF is powerful and why it is impractical in its pure form is what separates a memorized definition from real understanding.
